sentences: A statesman, the Prime Minister, and a minister, the Secretary of State for European Affairs, come to the detective in the matter of a document stolen from the minister's dispatch box, which he kept at home in a city street when not at work.
If divulged, this document could bring about very dire consequences for all of the continent, even war.

They are loath to tell the detective at first the exact nature of the document's contents, but when the detective declines to take on their case, they tell him it was a rather injudicious letter from a foreign potentate.
It disappeared from the dispatch box one evening when the minister's wife was out at the theatre for four hours.
No one in the house knew about the document, not even the Secretary's wife.
None of the servants could have guessed what was in the box.
The detective decides to begin with some spies known to him and is then astonished to hear from the doctor that one of those that he names, a certain agent, has been murdered.
Before the detective has a chance to act, the lady, the European Secretary's wife, arrives unexpectedly at the detective's lodgings.
She asks the detective insistently about the stolen document's contents, but the detective only reveals there would be regrettable consequences if the document were not found.
The lady also begs the detective to tell her husband nothing of her visit.
The detective's spy hunt does not go well.
Four days after the murder, French police arrest the probable murderer of the agent: a Frenchwoman, whom the agent married in the French capital under an alias.
She was seen in the city near the agent's house the night of the crime, but she is now useless as a witness because she has gone insane.
The inspector calls the detective to the murder scene to examine something odd.
The agent bled over a drugget, and the blood soaked through it, but curiously there is no bloodstain on the floor under the drugget.
However, there is one under the opposite edge of the carpet.
It can only mean that the constable guarding the crime scene has been foolish enough to let someone in and leave them alone while they moved things in the room, including the carpet.
The detective tells the inspector to take the constable to a back room and obtain a confession, which he does vigorously.
Meanwhile, the detective pulls the unfastened carpet aside and quickly finds a hiding place in the floor, but it is empty.
The errant constable tells the detective that the unauthorised visitor was a young woman.
She apparently fainted at the sight of the blood but had left while the constable went out to fetch some brandy to revive her.
As the detective is leaving the agent's house, he shows the constable a photograph, and he recognises it as the visitor.
The detective goes to the minister's household and confronts the lady, accusing her of the theft.
At first, she denies everything, but is forced to admit her wrongdoing under the threat of certain scandal.
The lady admits the agent was blackmailing her with a compromising letter written by her years earlier, and demanded the document as payment (an unnamed spy had made the agent aware of the document).
The lady went to the agent's house to do the business when, as it happened, his wife from the French capital showed up and confronted him about his affair, believing the lady was his mistress.
The lady hurriedly left, albeit not before seeing the agent place the document under the drugget.
She returned to fetch the document after her visit to the detective convinced her she needed to do so.
She hands the document to the detective.
At the detective's suggestion, the document is put back in the dispatch box using the lady's duplicate key.

When the minister arrives back home with the Prime Minister, the detective pretends to believe that the evidence has convinced him that the document must still be in the box, shuffled between other papers.
It is soon found, and the minister rejoices that it was apparently only a mistake.
The Prime Minister suspects the detective knows more than he is telling, but the detective simply responds, "We also have our diplomatic secrets."
The detective is visited by a gentleman, who wishes to discuss something "grotesque".
No sooner has he arrived at the detective's lodgings than a police inspector also shows up, along with a second inspector of the county constabulary.
They wish a statement from the gentleman about the murder of his host near a village the previous night.

The gentleman explains that he spent the night at a country lodge, the host's rented house, but when he woke up in the morning, he found that the host and his servants had all disappeared, leaving him alone in the house.
The gentleman mentions that a note, delivered during dinner the previous evening, had caused great consternation to the host and may have had some connection with the household's disappearance.

The story told by him seems inconsistent with the physical evidence, yet the policemen never doubt his story, demonstrating to the detective that the gentleman must have been invited to provide a fake alibi, which would have carried much weight by virtue of him being an extremely proper and respectable gentleman.
The detective's investigation leads him to a neighbouring household, whose master has spent time in the tropics, and whose secretary is a dark-skinned foreigner.
The detective believes that the cryptic note came from this household and the writer could only be the house's governess, a certain lady, who has not been seen since the night of the murder.
That night, the householder's family flee by train.
The governess escapes with the help of a former gardener.
It is revealed that "the householder" is in fact a tyrant, an overthrown dictator from a tropical region who left a bloody trail behind as he escaped to the island nation.
The governess's real name is that of a diplomat's wife.
Her late husband was his republic's ambassador to the island nation and a potential political rival to the tyrant.
The tyrant had him recalled and shot so that he would not pose a threat to the tyrant's position.
Fortunately, the diplomat's wife stayed behind in the island nation and avoided harm herself.
She went on to change her name and secure the position as governess to the householder's children in order to get closer to and spy on him.
The tyrant and his secretary give the police the slip in the capital, and resurface in a foreign city under new aliases.
However, they are both murdered, and their killers are never caught.
A woman, a landlady, comes to the detective's lodgings with some questions about her new lodger, who is renting a room on the top floor of her house.

A youngish, heavily bearded man, who spoke good but accented English, came to her and offered double her usual rent on the condition that he receive a key to the house and was not to be disturbed for any reason.
He went out the first night that he was there, and came back after midnight when the rest of the household had gone to bed.
Since then, neither the landlady, her husband, nor their servant girl has seen him.
He requests items via printed notes, and his meals are to be left on a chair outside the door.
After the landlady leaves, the detective remarks to the doctor that it seems likely that the person in the landlady's house is not the bearded man who made the arrangements.
The detective determines that messages are being sent to the lodger in the form of advertisements placed in a particular newspaper, which the landlady leaves by the door each morning.
The detective and the doctor go to the landlady's house and spy on the lodger, who they discover to be a young woman with a dark complexion.
That evening, the detective and the doctor are on hand to see her confederate send messages by a waving candle.
The detective and the doctor meet a police inspector and a private agency detective from a foreign country.
They are lying in wait for a gangster, a vicious killer.
Upon entering the room from which the signal originated, they discover the gangster lying on the floor in a pool of blood, dead from a stab wound to the throat.
The lodger is revealed as a young wife, and her confederate is a young man, her husband.

She confirms that the couple were seeking refuge from the gangster, who was out to kill the husband for betraying the brotherhood, a secret Italian criminal organization to which they had both belonged.
The husband decided to leave the organization in spite of the threatened consequences.
He and his wife fled their homeland and went to a city abroad to escape the brotherhood, but the gangster tracked the husband down and attacked while he was trying to signal the wife.
The inspector takes the wife down to the police station, but comments that she and the husband will likely face no criminal charges over the gangster's death.
The monotony of the thick smog-shrouded city is broken by a sudden visit from the detective's brother.
He has come about some missing, secret submarine plans.
Seven of the ten plans have been found with a young man's body, but the three "most essential" papers are still missing.
The young man was a young clerk in a government office at a military arsenal, whose body was found next to the underground railway tracks near a certain tube station, his head crushed.
He had little money with him (although there appears to have been no robbery), theatre tickets, and curiously, no underground railway ticket.
The inspector tells the detective that a passenger reported hearing a thud, as though a body had fallen on the track, close to where the young man's body was found.
The passenger could not see anything, however, owing to the thick fog.

After an examination of the track near that station, the detective concludes that the young man had been killed elsewhere, was deposited on the roof of an underground railway train, and fell off when the jarring action of going across a railway point at that station shook the coach.
The detective decides to visit an official, who was in charge of the papers.
He has, however, died, apparently of a broken heart from the loss of his honour when the papers were stolen, according to his brother the colonel.

On visiting the young man's fiancée, the detective learns that the young man had something on his mind for the last week or so of his life; he had commented on how easily a traitor could get hold of "the secret" and how much foreign agents would pay for it.
On the night in question, the young man and his fiancée were on their way to the theatre, when he suddenly dashed off into the fog and did not return.
The detective next goes to the office from which the plans were stolen.
One employee, the senior clerk, tells the detective that, as always, he was the last man out of the office that night, and that he had put the papers in the safe.

Anyone coming in afterwards to steal them would have needed three keys (for the building, the office, and the safe), but no duplicates were found on the young man's body, and only the late official had all three keys.
The senior clerk also mentions that one of the seven recovered papers includes a unique invention, without which the submarine could not be properly built.
The detective also discovers that it is possible to see what is happening inside the office from outside, as the iron shutters do not close properly.
After leaving, the detective finds that the clerk at the nearby underground railway station remembers seeing the young man on the evening in question.
Deeply shaken by something, he had taken a train to another station in the city.

Acting on information from his brother, and on what he has learnt thus far, the detective identifies a person of interest: a spy, a known foreign agent who left town shortly after the young man's murder.

Some small reconnaissance shows the detective that the spy's house backs onto an above-ground portion of the underground railway line; furthermore, owing to traffic at a nearby junction, trains often stop right under his windows.
It seems clear that the young man's body was laid on the train roof just there.
The detective and the doctor break into the spy's empty house and closely examine the windows, finding that the grime has been smudged, and there is a bloodstain.
An underground train stops right under the window.
Some messages from a newspaper's agony column, all seeming to allude to a business deal, are also found, posted by "the pseudonym".
The detective posts a similarly cryptic message in the newspaper demanding a meeting, signing it with the pseudonym, in the hopes that the thief might show up at the spy's house.
The colonel shows up and is stunned to find the detective, the doctor, the inspector, and the detective's brother all waiting for him.
He confesses to the theft of the plans, but swears that it was the spy who killed the young man.
The young man had followed the colonel to the spy's and then intervened, and the spy had dealt the young man a fatal blow to the head.
The spy then decided, over the colonel's objections, that he had to keep three of the papers, because they could not be copied in a short time.
He then got the idea of putting the other seven in the young man's pocket and putting him on a train roof outside his window, reasoning that he would be blamed for the theft when his body was found.
Deep in debt, the colonel had acted out of a need for money.
He redeems himself somewhat by agreeing to write to the spy, whose address abroad he knows, inviting him to come back to the country for the fourth, vital page.
This ruse also works; the spy is imprisoned, and the missing pages of the plans are recovered from his trunk.
The colonel dies in prison, not long after starting his sentence.
For his efforts, the detective is given an emerald tie pin by "a certain gracious lady", implied to be the queen, as the pin was received at a royal residence in the 1890s.
The doctor is called to tend the detective, who is apparently dying of a rare tropical disease, an exotic fever, contracted while he was on a case.
The doctor is shocked, not having heard about his friend's illness.
The landlady says that the detective has neither eaten nor drunk anything in three days.
The detective instructs the doctor not to come near him, because the illness is highly infectious.
In fact, he scorns to be treated by the doctor and insults his abilities, astonishing and hurting the doctor.
Although the doctor wishes to examine the detective himself or call in a specialist, the detective demands that the doctor wait several hours before seeking help.
While the doctor waits, he examines several objects in the detective's room.
The detective grows angry when the doctor touches a small ivory box, ordering the doctor to put it down and sit still.
At six o'clock, the detective tells the doctor to turn the gaslight on, but only half-full.

He then instructs the doctor to bring a certain gentleman of a house in another street to see the detective, but to make sure that the doctor returns to the detective's lodgings before the gentleman arrives.
The doctor goes to the gentleman's address.
Although the gentleman refuses to see anyone, the doctor forces his way in.
Once the doctor explains his errand on behalf of the detective, the gentleman's attitude changes drastically.
The gentleman agrees to come to the detective's lodgings within a half hour.

The doctor excuses himself, saying that he has another appointment; he returns before the gentleman's arrival and, at the detective's instruction, conceals himself behind the head of the detective's bed.
Believing that they are alone, the gentleman is frank with the detective.
It emerges, to the hiding doctor's horror, that the detective has been sickened by the same illness that killed the gentleman's nephew.
The gentleman then sees the little ivory box, which he had sent to the detective by post, and which contains a sharp spring infected with the illness.
The gentleman pockets it, removing the evidence of his crime.
He then resolves to stay there and watch the detective die.
The detective asks the gentleman to turn the gas up full, which the gentleman does.
The gentleman then asks the detective if he would like anything else, to which the detective replies - no longer in the voice of a man near death - "a match and a cigarette."
A police inspector then enters, as the full gaslight was the signal to move in.
The detective tells the inspector to arrest the gentleman for the murder of his nephew, and perhaps also for the attempted murder of the detective himself.

The gentleman points out that his word is as good as the detective's in court, but the detective then calls for the doctor to emerge from hiding, to present himself as another witness to the conversation.
The detective explains that he feigned his illness as a ruse to induce the gentleman to confess to his nephew's murder.
The detective was not infected by the little box, having learned to take precautions about his incoming mail due to the number of enemies he has made.

Starving himself for three days and the claim of the "disease's" infectious nature was to keep the doctor from examining him and discovering the ruse, since, as he clarifies, he has every respect for his friend's medical skills.
The detective sends the doctor to a lakeside town to investigate a lady's disappearance since he himself is too busy in the capital.
The lady is a lone, unwed woman denied a rich inheritance on account of her sex.
She does, however, carry valuable jewels with her.
It is also her habit to write to her old governess, an elderly woman, every other week, but for the past five weeks, there has not been a word from her.
She has left the hotel in the lakeside town for parts unknown.
Her last two bank transactions were cheques, one to pay her hotel bill, and another for £50 to her maid, a young woman.
In the mountain country, the doctor finds out that the lady stayed at the hotel for several weeks, but then suddenly left in a hurry one day.
Only one witness could suggest an explanation, one involving a big, bearded man who kept hounding her.
It also emerges that the lady's maid has left her employ, although it is not known why.
The doctor finds out where the lady went, and inquires at an inn in a spa town, in a neighbouring country.
She stayed there for a fortnight and met a couple described as a devout man, a convalescent missionary and biblical scholar from a distant continent, and his wife.
The lady left with them three weeks ago for the capital, and nothing has been heard of her since.
The doctor also finds out that the big bearded man, the "savage", came about a week ago looking for her.
The doctor telegraphs the detective about his progress, and oddly, the detective wires back asking for a description of the missionary's left ear.
The doctor believes this to be the detective's attempt at humour.
The detective is actually in earnest.
The doctor visits the young woman, the former maid, in a southern town, in a third country, and it turns out that her upcoming wedding was why she left the lady's employ.
The £50 was a wedding present.
She, too, believes that the bearded man was the reason that her former mistress left the lakeside town.
He was quite a rough man.
During this interview, the young woman sees the very man in question in the street.
The doctor rushes out and demands to know who he is and what he has done with the lady.
A fight ensues and the doctor is nearly strangled.
A French workman breaks the fight up with his cudgel and the bearded man withdraws.

It then turns out that the workman is the disguised detective, who suggests that the doctor accompany him back to the capital, and wryly observes that there is no blunder which the doctor has failed to commit in this investigation.
Before leaving, however, the detective interviews someone.
It is the bearded man, a gentleman of good family, an old suitor of the lady's.
Yes, he is seeking the lady, but he still wants to win her heart.
As a younger man, despite being the son of a famous Admiral, he was not rich.
Now that he has made his fortune in a distant colony, he hopes she will see him differently, but he is still rather churlish and clearly the lady is unwilling.
The detective recommends that he go back to the capital.
Once the detective and the doctor are back at the detective's lodgings, the detective reads a telegram from the spa town about the missionary's left ear—"jagged or torn".
This confirms the detective's suspicion that the missionary is in fact a notorious swindler, a vicious rascal from a far-off land (his earlobe was chewed away in a bar brawl).
His so-called wife's real name is that of a known accomplice.
He beguiles young women by playing to their religious beliefs, as the missionary did with the lady.
This suggested his true identity to the detective.
The detective believes that the lady is in the capital, and quite possibly dead, or if not, confined in some way.
The search seems hopeless.
The police follow known associates, the detective places advertisements hoping to learn something, but nothing happens.
Then, a pawnshop reports that someone matching the missionary's description has pawned a pendant very much like one owned by the lady.
The detective and the doctor find themselves at a coastal village in a remote county one spring.
The holiday is interrupted when the local vicar and his lodger visit the detective, asking for his assistance.
The night before, the lodger had gone to visit his three siblings, played whist with them, and then left.
The next morning, the housekeeper found the trio still sitting in their places at the table; the brothers had gone insane, and the sister was dead.
A traveller, a famous hunter-explorer and a cousin of the family, aborts his sailing from a port town after the vicar wires him with the tragic news.
He asks the detective what his suspicions are, and is displeased when the detective will not voice any.
The next morning, the vicar informs the detective that the lodger has died in the same way as his sister.
The two men, along with the doctor, rush to the lodger's room.
A lamp is lit and smoking on the table beside the dead man.

The detective deduces that a poison, activated by combustion and affecting the cognitive functions, is the murder weapon; a fire was burning in the first murder room and a lamp in the second, and people who entered them either felt ill or fainted.

After a dangerous experiment in which he tests the residue of the poison on himself and is only just rescued by the doctor, the detective reveals that the lodger is guilty of the first crime and further deduces that the explorer was the lodger's murderer.
The explorer confesses that he held the lodger at gunpoint and forced him to breathe the poison.
It comes from a plant known by a sinister name.

The explorer once described the powder to the lodger, who stole some from the explorer's collection of African curiosities, then attempted to murder his siblings by throwing it on the fire just before he left.
It is revealed that the explorer was passionately in love with the sister, but was still married to and unable to divorce his first wife who had abandoned him years ago.
The detective's sympathies in this matter lie with the explorer, and he tells him to go back to his work in a distant continent and never return.
On the eve of a great war, the German agent is getting ready to leave the country with his vast collection of intelligence, gathered over a four-year period.
His wife and household have already left one port for another port in a neighbouring country, leaving only him and his elderly English housekeeper.

The German agent's associate, a baron, a German diplomat from his country's embassy, is impressed by his acquisition of vital British military secrets, and tells the German agent that he will be received in his home capital as a hero.
The German agent says that he is waiting for one last transaction with his Irish-American informant, who will arrive shortly with a rich treasure: naval signals.
The baron leaves just before the informant arrives.
The German agent's housekeeper has turned her light off and retired.
The informant shows the German agent a package.
The informant disparages the German agent's safe, but the German agent proudly says that its construction and the double combination lock make it impenetrable.
He tells the informant that the combination is "August 1914".
The informant, mentioning cases in which several German informants have ended up in prison, is distrustful of the German agent and refuses to deliver the naval codes until he receives payment.
The German agent refuses to pay until he has examined the informant's intelligence data.
The informant hands him the package.
The German agent finds that it is a book titled as a manual on beekeeping, hardly what he expected.
Even less expected is the chloroform-soaked rag that is held in his face by the informant a moment later.
The informant is actually the detective in disguise, and the chauffeur who brought him is the doctor.

Now past their heyday, they have nonetheless caught several spies (the detective is actually responsible for the imprisoned agents of whom "the informant" spoke), and fed the Germans some thoroughly untrustworthy intelligence.
The detective had retired from detective work, spending his days beekeeping in the countryside, but returned after the Foreign Minister and the Premier came to him.

The detective has been on this case for two years, and it has taken him to one foreign city, another foreign city, and a neighbouring island, where he learnt to play the part of a bitter Irish-American, even gaining the credentials of a member of a secret society.
He identified the security leak through which British secrets were reaching the Germans, and then set out to apprehend the receiving agents themselves.
The housekeeper was one of the detective's agents: the light that she switched off was the signal to the detective and the doctor that the coast was clear.
The detective and the doctor take the German agent and the evidence to police headquarters.
In reference to the impending War, the detective says, "There's an east wind coming, doctor."
The doctor misinterprets the meaning of the words and says, "I think not, detective.
It is very warm", to which the detective replies: "Good old doctor!
You are the one fixed point in a changing age.
There's an east wind coming all the same, such a wind as never blew on this country yet.
It will be cold and bitter, doctor, and a good many of us may wither before its blast.
But it's heaven's own wind none the less, and a cleaner, better, stronger land will lie in the sunshine when the storm has cleared."
The doctor arrives in the detective's lodgings where the page boy shows him a wax effigy of the detective placed near a curtained window in the sitting room.
The effigy produces a shadow on the curtain that, when viewed from outside, is the unmistakable profile of the detective.
Using this visual trick, the detective aims to give a perfect target to a would-be murderer with a rifle.
The detective names his murderer as a certain count, the diamond thief he has been following in disguise.
He gives the criminal's address to the doctor, then sends the doctor out the back for the police.
As the Count arrives, the detective has the page boy invite him inside, then takes him by surprise when he attempts an assault on the effigy.
The detective then offers the Count and his helper, a boxer, freedom if they give up the jewel, or jail if not.
He invites them to discuss the deal while he plays violin in the next room.

When the Count decides to double-cross the detective and takes the stone from his secret pocket to show the boxer in window light, the detective springs from the chair in place of his replica and grabs the £100,000 jewel.
His bedroom has a gramophone and secret passage to behind the curtain.
After the police take away the villains, a nobleman – described by the detective as "the eminent peer who represents the very highest interests" – sweeps in.
Unlike the Prime Minister and Home Secretary, he did not want the detective.
When tricked into insisting on arrest for whoever is found possessing the diamond, he finds the jewel in his pocket – where the detective has placed it – and apologizes.
Finally, the detective can eat.
A millionaire, a gold magnate and former senator from "some Western state", approaches the detective to investigate the murder of his wife in order to clear his children's governess of the crime.
It soon emerges that the millionaire's marriage had been unhappy and he treated his wife very badly.
He had fallen in love with her when he met her in a South American country, but soon realised they had nothing in common.
He became attracted to the governess; since he could not marry her, he had attempted to please her in other ways, such as trying to help people less fortunate than himself.
The millionaire's wife was found lying in a pool of blood on the estate's bridge with a bullet through the head and note from the governess, agreeing to a meeting at that location, in her hand.
A recently discharged revolver with one shot fired is found in the governess's wardrobe.
The detective agrees to look at the situation in spite of the damning evidence.
From the outset, the detective observes some rather odd things about the case.
How could the governess so coolly and rationally have planned and carried out the murder and then carelessly tossed the murder weapon into her wardrobe?
What was the strange chip on the underside of the bridge's stone balustrade?
Why was the millionaire's wife clutching the note from the governess when she died?
If the murder weapon was one of a matched pair of pistols, why couldn't the other one be found in the millionaire's collection?

The detective uses his powers of deduction to solve the crime, and demonstrates, using the doctor's revolver, how it was perpetrated: the millionaire's wife, outraged and jealous of the governess's relationship with her husband, resolved to end her own life and frame her rival for the crime.

After arranging a meeting with the governess, requesting her to leave her response in a note, the millionaire's wife tied a rock on a piece of string to the end of a revolver, and shot herself, the rock pulling the revolver over the side of the bridge; the revolver found in the governess's wardrobe was the other pistol of the pair, which had been fired off in the woods earlier, and the chip in the bridge was caused by the pistol hitting the stonework as it was pulled off by the rock.
The detective's reconstruction reproduces the damage to the balustrade of the bridge.
He asks the police to drag the lake for the revolvers of the doctor and the millionaire.
